questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: The chapter defines hypocalcemia as serum calcium below ___ mg/dL.
questions.exp: The opening threshold is <8.4 mg/dL; interpret total calcium with albumin or measure ionized calcium where appropriate. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: After thyroid surgery, a patient develops circumoral tingling, twitching and stridor. Which mechanism makes this an immediate airway concern?
questions.exp: Acute hypocalcemia causes neuromuscular excitability and potentially fatal laryngeal spasm; chronic calcification does not explain the acute presentation. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: Match the following — 1) Acute cardiac effect 2) Acute CNS effect 3) Chronic ocular effect … A) Long QT B) Generalized tonic-clonic seizure C) Cataract
questions.exp: Acute manifestations include long QT and GTCS; cataract belongs to the chronic group. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: Which finding is the odd one out among the chapter's chronic hypocalcemia manifestations?
questions.exp: Laryngeal spasm is an acute excitability manifestation. Basal ganglia calcification, benign intracranial hypertension, cataract and dry skin are chronic features. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: A patient with longstanding hypoparathyroidism has symmetric deep gray-matter calcification on CT. Which site corresponds to the chapter's chronic hypocalcemia images?
questions.exp: The CT panels illustrate intracranial calcification associated with chronic hypocalcemia; the listed characteristic site is the basal ganglia. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: Tapping the facial nerve to provoke facial muscle twitching elicits ___ sign.
questions.exp: Chvostek's sign tests latent neuromuscular irritability by facial nerve percussion. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: Assess these statements: I A negative Chvostek sign excludes hypocalcemia. II Facial-nerve tapping elicits Trousseau carpopedal spasm.
questions.exp: A negative Chvostek response does not exclude hypocalcemia because sensitivity is poor. Facial tapping elicits Chvostek facial twitching; cuff inflation elicits Trousseau carpopedal spasm. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: A cuff is inflated 20 mmHg above systolic pressure and the hand assumes a carpopedal posture. Which sign has been elicited?
questions.exp: The cuff maneuver elicits Trousseau's sign, also called main d'accoucheur, and is different from the malignancy-associated eponym. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: A patient's systolic pressure is 118 mmHg. Using the chapter's latent-tetany maneuver, the cuff is inflated to approximately ___ mmHg.
questions.exp: The stated maneuver uses 20 mmHg above systolic pressure: 118 + 20 = 138. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: Which finding is not an example of apparent neuromuscular irritability listed here?
questions.exp: Tingling, twitching, fasciculations, circumoral paresthesia and tetany are apparent manifestations; cataract is chronic rather than an excitability sign. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: Hypocalcemia is followed by a prolonged QT and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which arrhythmia best fits this combination?
questions.exp: Long QT with polymorphic VT is the torsades pattern illustrated in the chapter. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
questions.q: At the standard ECG speed of 25 mm/s, assess: I Twelve small boxes correspond to 0.48 seconds. II The page's raw-QT box count replaces QTc assessment at every heart rate.
questions.exp: Each small box is 0.04 seconds, so 12 boxes equal 0.48 seconds. The page's >12-box illustration is not a substitute for rate-corrected QT interpretation. (Book p883)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: Two days after neck surgery, calcium is low, phosphate is high and PTH is suppressed. Which explanation best fits all three values?
questions.exp: Low calcium with high phosphate and low PTH identifies deficient PTH secretion; postsurgical disease is the most common cause listed. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: For hypocalcemia, the chapter first organizes causes using serum ___ and ___.
questions.exp: The cause tree is based on phosphate and PTH, after confirming true hypocalcemia. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: An adult with mucocutaneous candidiasis and ectodermal abnormalities develops low-PTH hypocalcemia without surgery. Which syndrome fits?
questions.exp: APECED means autoimmune polyendocrinopathy–candidiasis–ectodermal dystrophy and corresponds to APS/PGA type 1. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: Match the following DiGeorge clues — 1) Gene 2) Chromosomal region 3) Immune-organ defect … A) TBX1 B) Thymic hypoplasia C) 22q11.2 deletion
questions.exp: DiGeorge syndrome is linked to TBX1 and 22q deletion; thymic hypoplasia explains its immune component. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: Which is the odd one out in the CATCH22 feature set?
questions.exp: CATCH22 comprises cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate and hypocalcemia with 22q deletion; deficient parathyroid development, not hyperplasia, explains the calcium finding. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: A neonate has a conotruncal heart defect, cleft palate and hypocalcemic seizures. Which additional finding most strongly supports the same syndrome?
questions.exp: This is the CATCH22 constellation of DiGeorge syndrome; thymic hypoplasia is the discriminating associated finding. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: Evaluate: I CKD-related secondary HPT requires suppressed PTH. II Low calcium with high phosphate and high PTH can occur in CKD.
questions.exp: The elevated PTH is a compensatory response in CKD, unlike low-PTH hypoparathyroidism. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: Match the following — 1) Postsurgical gland loss 2) CKD secondary HPT 3) AKI … A) Low Ca/high phosphate with high PTH B) Low Ca/high phosphate with acute renal dysfunction C) Low Ca/high phosphate with low PTH
questions.exp: The page separates deficient secretion after surgery from secondary HPT in CKD and the acute renal failure branch. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: Which cause does not belong in the cellular-stress branch of hypocalcemia with phosphate release?
questions.exp: Tumor lysis, muscle breakdown and hemolysis release intracellular phosphate. Isolated gland excision instead reduces PTH secretion. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: A patient with abdominal pain and vomiting is found to have acute pancreatitis and low calcium. Which interpretation follows the chapter's warning?
opts: Low calcium rules out pancreatitis as the underlying diagnosis
Pancreatitis must suppress PTH to cause these symptoms
Symptoms may resemble hypercalcemia despite a low measured calcium
Abdominal symptoms establish hypercalcemia despite the result
questions.exp: The page warns that pancreatitis can mimic hypercalcemic abdominal symptoms while investigations show hypocalcemia. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
questions.q: In the low-calcium/high-phosphate branch with normal or raised PTH, the non-cell-lysis systemic infection listed is ___.
questions.exp: Sepsis appears beside cellular stress and pancreatitis in the normal/high-PTH branch; the tree does not imply that every cause has identical phosphate values in every patient. (Book p884)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Match the following drug mechanisms — 1) Citrate 2) Bisphosphonate 3) Cisplatin … A) Calcium complexing B) Inhibition of bone resorption C) Tubular injury with electrolyte loss
questions.exp: Citrate complexes calcium; bisphosphonates reduce calcium release from bone; cisplatin belongs to the tubular-injury group. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Which drug is the odd one out in the page's renal tubular-injury subgroup causing hypocalcemia?
questions.exp: Calcitonin lowers calcium through its hormonal antiresorptive action; the other three are grouped under tubular injury. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: A patient has repeatedly low total calcium but marked hypoalbuminemia. What is the first step in the chapter's exclusion sequence?
questions.exp: The sequence begins with confirming corrected calcium, then ruling out magnesium deficiency, then evaluating hypoparathyroidism and other causes. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: After confirming true hypocalcemia, the deficiency to exclude before assigning primary parathyroid failure is ___.
questions.exp: Magnesium deficiency can impair PTH secretion and action, so it precedes hypoparathyroidism in the sequence. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Following parathyroidectomy, calcium and phosphate both fall while ALP rises. Which postoperative mechanism fits best?
questions.exp: Hungry bone syndrome takes calcium and phosphate into bone and is accompanied by increased matrix synthesis/ALP. Gland failure tends to raise phosphate. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Assess: I Hungry bone syndrome characteristically raises phosphate. II The postoperative hypoparathyroidism row shows high phosphate, markedly low PTH and normal ALP.
questions.exp: Hungry bone lowers both calcium and phosphate and raises ALP; the PTH cell is blank. Postsurgical hypoparathyroidism instead shows phosphate up, PTH markedly down and normal ALP. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: In the postoperative graph, the calcium curve drops while the ALP curve rises. Which interpretation best explains why the curves diverge?
opts: Reduced ALP synthesis from hepatic failure
Persistent calcium release from active osteolysis
Analytical correction for falling albumin alone
Bone mineral uptake with increased matrix activity
questions.exp: The graph illustrates hungry bone after parathyroidectomy: mineral uptake lowers calcium while osteoblastic activity raises ALP. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Match the following hungry-bone graph labels — 1) Left vertical axis 2) Right vertical axis 3) Horizontal axis … A) ALP in U/L B) Days around the operative course C) Adjusted calcium in mg/dL
questions.exp: The left axis is adjusted calcium, the right ALP and the horizontal axis time in days. The scan labels days after parathyroidectomy but places its operative arrow after zero, so the qualitative postoperative trend is more reliable than inferring an exact operative day. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: In the illustrated perioperative course, zoledronate and elcatonin precede surgery. Which subsequent supplement combination is annotated?
opts: IV calcium and magnesium with oral calcitriol
IV phosphate and potassium with oral calcitonin
IV calcium and phosphate with oral cholecalciferol
IV magnesium and bicarbonate with oral cinacalcet
questions.exp: The graph annotates IV calcium 3–5 g/day and magnesium 2–6 g/day with oral calcitriol 1–3 µg/day. These are case-figure annotations, not universal replacement doses; formulations, elemental content and renal function must be checked. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Assess the graph reference bands: I Adjusted calcium is marked normal at 8.5–10.3 mg/dL. II ALP 68–430 U/L is explicitly labeled for a 16-year-old male rather than every adult.
questions.exp: The graph prints calcium 8.5–10.3 mg/dL and ALP 68–430 U/L for a 16-year-old male. Age-dependent ALP ranges must not be applied universally. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: The molecular chain in pseudohypoparathyroidism is a ___ mutation causing defective ___ signaling.
questions.exp: GNAS defects alter Gsα signaling and produce resistance to PTH action, rather than simply absent hormone secretion. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: A child has hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia and a markedly elevated PTH despite preserved renal function. Which mechanism should be considered?
opts: Activating renal CaSR with suppressed PTH
Autonomous PTH secretion from an adenoma
questions.exp: PHP produces low calcium, high phosphate and high PTH because target tissues resist the hormone. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Match the following — 1) PHP type Ia 2) PHP type Ib 3) PHP type II … A) No AHO, complete PTH resistance B) AHO, complete PTH resistance C) No AHO, preserved cAMP rise
questions.exp: The table distinguishes Ia by AHO, Ib by absent AHO, and type II by a cAMP rise despite a downstream response defect. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Exogenous PTH raises urinary cAMP, but the expected phosphaturic response is impaired. Which PHP subtype fits the table?
questions.exp: Type II has a preserved cAMP rise with a downstream signaling defect; the source calls its resistance partial. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Evaluate the table's other-hormone-resistance row: I PHP Ia is positive. II PHP Ib is marked variable (+/−).
questions.exp: The table marks other hormone resistance as + in Ia, +/− in Ib and absent in type II and PPHP. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Match the following phenotype patterns — 1) Maternal GNAS defect with resistance 2) Paternal GNAS defect without resistance 3) PHP Ib … A) AHO with PHP Ia B) AHO absent C) AHO with pseudo-PHP
questions.exp: Parent-of-origin distinguishes maternal PHP Ia from paternal PPHP; PHP Ib lacks the AHO phenotype in the table. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: Which disorder is the odd one out for the low-calcium/high-phosphate/high-PTH biochemical triad?
questions.exp: PPHP has an AHO phenotype without the biochemical PTH resistance seen in the PHP groups. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: A patient has AHO from a paternal GNAS defect but normal calcium, phosphate and PTH. What response to administered PTH is expected?
questions.exp: The table also labels PPHP resistance as normal and its biochemical triad absent. PPHP should not be taught as a failed PTH/cAMP response on the basis of the ambiguous 'no change' cell. (Book p885)

questions.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
questions.q: The table's reduced-Gsα row is positive in ___ and ___, but negative in Ib and II.
questions.exp: The printed row refers to reduced Gsα, a signaling protein rather than a 'Gsα receptor'; it marks Ia and PPHP positive. (Book p885)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: Which feature is the odd one out for Albright hereditary osteodystrophy?
questions.exp: AHO features shortened metacarpals, short stature, round facies and cognitive impairment, not long slender digits. (Book p886)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: The AHO summary emphasizes shortening of the fourth ___ more than the corresponding ___.
questions.exp: The handwritten summary states short fourth metacarpal > metatarsal. (Book p886)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: Match the following clenched-fist patterns — 1) Down syndrome 2) Turner syndrome 3) PHP Ia … A) Fourth-knuckle dimple B) Fourth- and fifth-knuckle dimples C) Third-knuckle dimple
questions.exp: The diagrams pair Down syndrome with the third metacarpal, Turner syndrome with the fourth and PHP Ia with the fourth and fifth. (Book p886)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: A child with round facies and short stature makes a fist showing 'knuckle, knuckle, dimple, dimple.' Which diagnosis is favored by the illustrated pattern?
questions.exp: Fourth- and fifth-metacarpal shortening produces the PHP Ia knuckle pattern in the figure. (Book p886)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: Assess: I A normal clenched fist has a fourth-knuckle dimple. II An isolated fourth-knuckle dimple establishes PHP Ia.
questions.exp: The normal diagram shows four knuckles; the Turner diagram also has a fourth-knuckle dimple, so an isolated dimple is not specific for PHP Ia. (Book p886)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: A patient has severe symptomatic acute hypocalcemia with tetany. Which replacement is the chapter's initial intravenous option?
questions.exp: The page selects IV 10% calcium gluconate for acute symptomatic disease, rather than the listed oral salts. (Book p886)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: What volume and concentration constitute the chapter's initial calcium gluconate ampoule?
questions.exp: The source specifies 10 mL (one ampoule) of 10% calcium gluconate. Its rapid 2–3-minute timing should not be used as an unmonitored clinical protocol; follow ECG-monitored local guidance. (Book p886)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: The continuation regimen printed here places 5 g calcium gluconate in ___ of ___ solution.
questions.exp: The source lists 5 g in 500 mL of 5% dextrose, with elemental-calcium dosing separately expressed per kilogram per hour. Do not confuse salt mass with elemental calcium. (Book p886)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: For the source's infusion notation, assess: I The rate is expressed as 1–3 mg elemental calcium/kg/hour. II Five grams of calcium gluconate means five grams of elemental calcium.
questions.exp: The page explicitly labels the rate as elemental calcium; the calcium gluconate salt mass is not the elemental calcium mass. A clinical infusion requires monitoring and a validated protocol. (Book p886)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: For acute symptomatic hypocalcemia, which initial calcium gluconate administration best follows monitored clinical guidance rather than the scan’s unusually rapid 2–3-minute line?
opts: 10–20 mL of 1% solution over about 10 minutes without ECG monitoring
1–2 mL of 10% solution over about 60 minutes with ECG monitoring
10–20 mL of 10% solution over about 10 minutes with ECG monitoring
10–20 mL of 10% solution as an unmonitored immediate bolus
questions.exp: The source prints 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate over 2–3 minutes, then an infusion over 5 hours. Contemporary product/local guidance uses 10–20 mL of 10% over about 10 minutes with ECG and calcium monitoring; the source timing is not a safe standalone protocol. See the calcium-gluconate SmPC and GGC guideline linked in REPORT_CH36-40.md. (Book p886)

questions.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
questions.q: The page's oral calcium ceiling is ___ per day.
questions.exp: Oral calcium up to 2 g/day is the source's adjunct entry; oral therapy is not a replacement for monitored IV treatment of severe symptomatic hypocalcemia. (Book p886)

units.title: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs
units.sec: Hypocalcemia: presentation and bedside signs · p883
units.guide: Distinguish acute excitability, long QT and seizures from chronic calcification, cataract and dry skin. Elicit latent tetany with facial tapping or cuff inflation; the two tests are not interchangeable. ECG intervals require rate correction in clinical use.

units.title: Hypocalcemia: phosphate–PTH cause branches
units.guide: Use phosphate and PTH together: low PTH suggests deficient secretion; normal/high PTH directs attention to renal failure, cell injury and other causes. DiGeorge: TBX1/22q11.2 and CATCH22; adult autoimmune disease: APECED.

units.title: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance
units.sec: Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance · p885
units.guide: Confirm corrected/ionized calcium, assess magnesium, then evaluate PTH. Compare hungry bone with gland failure. Read PHP types across biochemical resistance, cAMP response and AHO, while recognizing the printed PPHP response wording is misleading.

units.title: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment
units.sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment · p886
units.guide: AHO combines brachydactyly, short stature, round facies and cognitive impairment. Separate 3rd-, 4th-, and 4th/5th-knuckle patterns. Source calcium regimens are learning references, not unmonitored prescribing instructions.
